title: The ten words (Exodus 20:1–17)
hookLine: I am the Lord thy God who brought thee out: freedom comes before the rules

lines: IT DOESN'T START WITH A RULE.
cards: Recite the Ten Commandments from memory and notice where you begin. Thou shalt not, maybe. The text begins somewhere else.

The first thing God says from the mountain isn't a rule at all. It's a sentence about the past: who's speaking, and what that speaker has already done. And Exodus itself doesn't call them commandments.

teach.h: I BROUGHT THEE OUT. THEN: THE LAW.
teach.b: First, the opening line, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." Only then: "Thou shalt not have strange gods before me." The order matters.
God doesn't say, keep these rules and I'll free you. God says, I already freed you; here's how free people live. The commandments describe freedom; they aren't the price of it.

In Hebrew they're the aseret ha-devarim, the ten words or ten sayings; the Greek gave us Decalogue, from the same idea. Third, the counting. The text has more than ten sentences, so traditions divide them differently.
Catholics and Lutherans follow a division that goes back to Saint Augustine: no other gods and no carved images make one commandment, and coveting a neighbor's wife and coveting his goods make two.
Orthodox and Reformed churches, among others, count the images as a separate commandment and the coveting as one. In Jewish tradition the first word is the opening line itself, I am the Lord thy God.

teach.h: ONE TEXT, DIFFERENT WAYS TO COUNT.
teach.b: Same text, different ways of counting, and nobody's list is missing anything. Fourth, the shape.
Love of God comes first, then the rest turns to people: parents, life, marriage, property, truth, desire.
The Catechism says the ten words are meant to be read inside the story of the Exodus: they mark out the life of a people set free.
Deuteronomy's version ties the Sabbath to exactly that: remember that you were a servant in Egypt. Free people get a day of rest, by command.

how: Catholics often examine their conscience before confession by going through the Ten Commandments one at a time, following the numbering found in the Catechism, which traces back to Saint Augustine.

games.q: you're standing at the foot of Sinai. the voice from the mountain is about to speak for the first time. what comes first?
o: I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of Egypt.
games.why: a rescue, not a rule. God names what's already been done, then says how free people live.

practice: Pick one commandment and turn it around: instead of a fence, hear it as a gift to someone.

Thou shalt not steal is a gift to your neighbor, their things are safe with you; keep holy the Sabbath is a gift to you, one day you don't have to produce anything; honor your father and mother is a gift to people growing old.
If you pray, thank God for that one gift; if you don't, just notice who it protects.

wordCard.voice: Decalogue. The Greek name for the ten words God spoke at Sinai, which open not with a rule but with a rescue from Egypt. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the ten words, the Bible's own name for the commandments (Exodus 34:28).

carryVoice: Your line: freedom first, then the law. The rescue came before a single rule. Day three hundred seventy-eight, done.
